messages.subject: Dispersal Events_results
parts:
Hi everyone!

I am working with dispersal events matrices, considering different time slices and 6 regions.
I realized that, for all regions, the number of dispersal events increased a lot in the last period (towards to the present). See the attached figure. However, in my distance matrices, I did not consider any connection among regions in the last millions of years. So, I would expect a decrease in dispersal events in the present.

Anyone would know how to explain that? Maybe if there is a high similarity of species among all regions (i.e., high dispersal events in the past), it could cause the extremely high dispersal events in the present time. What do you think?

Thanks in advance!
Fernanda

parts:
Hi Fernanda,

A few quick thoughts:

On Fri, Apr 3, 2020 at 3:59 AM Fernanda Cassemiro <fernanda...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi everyone!

I am working with dispersal events matrices, considering different time slices and 6 regions.
I realized that, for all regions, the number of dispersal events increased a lot in the last period (towards to the present). See the attached figure. However, in my distance matrices, I did not consider any connection among regions in the last millions of years. So, I would expect a decrease in dispersal events in the present.

Anyone would know how to explain that? Maybe if there is a high similarity of species among all regions (i.e., high dispersal events in the past), it could cause the extremely high dispersal events in the present time. What do you think?

Unless you literally set the manual_dispersal_multiplier matrix to have "0" between all regions for the last few million years, then dispersal is possible during that time.

A few things will affect the number of dispersals observed:

1. All (living) phylogenies have more branches and more branch-length towards the present than they have anywhere else. So, the dispersal counts are likely to be highest towards the tips (just like there will be more recorded nodes for speciation events, etc.)

2. If you did estimate lots of dispersal deep in the tree, then this could push the d and/or j parameter to high values, and these high parameters could "force" some dispersal events even for recent clades where (say) parsimony would say none occurred. Combined with #1, this might produce a spike like you see.

3. Also, if you have some tips with widespread ranges (e.g. range ABC instead of A), then one common way the models would explain this is by invoking a bunch of "d" events on the tip branches.

My best bet, not knowing the dataset, would be a combination of #1 and #3.  Regardless, it is interesting you have a "hump" deeper back in time, that does suggest something interesting is going on.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.author: b6c73fdfb6befaf8
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Dispersal Events_results
parts:
Hi Nick!

Thanks very much for the prompt reply.

My phylogeny has more branch-length towards the present, and many tips with widespread ranges as well. The hump in the past is strictly correlated to important geological events in South America, which connected some regions in the past and boosted the dispersal. It's a really cool result.

Is there a way to solve this issue? Maybe if I calculate relative numbers of dispersal events by dividing absolute numbers by the total length of all branches within each time bin, it could minimize the peak of dispersal in the present.

Best,
Fernanda

Hi - yep, normalizing for the amount of preserved branch length seems like a reasonable option for me, then you are counting events-per-unit-of-branch-length.

Cheers!
Nick
